The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 targeted Chinese laborers, whose immigration was seen as endangering "good order."  
In the mid-to-late 19th century, Chinese immigrants to the United States were heavily involved in building the First Transcontinental Railroad (1860s), especially the Central Pacific Railroad.  
After the railroad's completion in 1869, many moved into other labor sectors, but the initial large influx was driven by demand for railroad labor.  
Gold mining (the California Gold Rush) attracted Chinese immigrants earlier (starting around 1850s), but by the 1870s railroad construction employed far more Chinese laborers in the West, fueling the demographic fears that prompted the 1882 law.  

Between gold mining and railroad construction, railroad construction was the larger employer of Chinese immigrants in the period immediately before the Act.
